content.title: Portugal Road Trip Itinerary (2 Weeks, 2026) – Porto to Algarve
content.text: Portugal looks small on a map… until you’re on Day 6, wondering how you’ve already filled your camera roll and your trunk. 😅 This 2-week Portugal road trip itinerary takes you from Porto in the north all the way down to the Algarve, with the best stops in between — Aveiro, Nazaré, Óbidos, Cascais, Sintra, Lisbon, Évora, and the cliffy beach goodness around Lagos. We’ve done Porto and Lisbon on separate trips before, and this was the trip where we finally connected it all properly by car — slow drives, scenic detours, and a few “wait… pull over, we need a photo” moments. To make this itinerary actually useful (not just inspirational), we’re sharing: a simple road trip map + route overview driving + toll tips (Portugal has electronic toll roads, so you’ll want to sort that early) where to stay in each base (with parking notes) and a day-by-day plan you can follow without overthinking it One quick heads-up from experience: we love having a car for the coast and smaller towns — but we wouldn’t bother driving around central Porto or Lisbon. Park it, then use your feet/metro/Uber and enjoy your life. Portugal Road Trip: Quick Overview (2 Weeks) At a glance Trip length: 14 days / 13 nights Route: Porto → Central Coast → Lisbon/Sintra → Évora → Algarve (Lagos base) Best for: first-timers who want cities + coast + a bit of countryside Do you need a car? For the full route, yes — but in Porto/Lisbon, not really (we park and explore on foot/metro). Tolls note (important): Portugal uses electronic toll roads, so make sure your rental is set up for toll payments (often via a Via Verde device). We cover the details in our guide to renting a car in Portugal. Map Portugal road trip map: Porto → Aveiro → Nazaré/Óbidos → Cascais/Cabo da Roca → Sintra → Lisbon → Évora → Costa Vicentina/Sagres → Lagos + Algarve day trips Where we recommend basing yourself (least stressful version) 📍2 nights Porto ➡️ Hotel Premium Porto Downtown — solid location near the historic centre + rooftop views. (Paid parking available.) 📍1 night Nazaré ➡️ Hotel Mar Bravo — beachfront, great for sunset + seafood, and parking included. 📍1 night Cascais ➡️ Eurostars Cascais — modern and comfortable with private parking. 📍4 nights Lisbon ➡️ Lumen Hotel— metro nearby, so you can ditch the car, rooftop pool, paid onsite parking. 📍2 nights Évora ➡️ Vintage Guest House — charming B&B feel, walkable, pool, private parking. 📍4 nights Lagos (Algarve base) ➡️ Casa das Praias — good-value base with a pool + free parking, easy for Algarve day trips. Quick route options Can you do it in reverse? Yep: Algarve → Lisbon → Porto works great too. Starting in Lisbon instead? Also, easy — you just flip the order. Short on time? We’ll add a tight 10-day version + 7-day Algarve-only version later in the post (this helps you pick up extra queries you’re already showing for). ➡️ If you’re still deciding whether to start your trip in Lisbon or Porto, we break down the pros and cons in our Porto vs Lisbon comparison — it can help you choose the most practical starting point. Day 1: Porto (Ribeira + Vila Nova de Gaia) Day 1 of our Portugal road trip itinerary starts in Porto — the perfect first stop for a 2 weeks in Portugal route. We keep it simple: views first, then the river, then wine (as nature intended). 😅 Morning: Dom Luís I Bridge + best first viewpoint Start at Dom Luís I Bridge and walk across the upper level for the best panoramic views over the Douro River and the red-roof chaos of Porto. If you do one thing early, make it this — it’s the quickest way to feel like you’ve “arrived”. Right after, pop to Jardim do Morro viewpoint (literally a few minutes away). It’s one of the easiest “wow” spots in Porto and a perfect place for your first photos. Practical tip (from us trying to be clever and failing): Porto’s streets are steep, and parking can be annoying. If you have a car already, leave it at your hotel or a paid garage and do Day 1 on foot. Jardim do Morro viewpoint. Early afternoon: WOW (World of Wine) All the best itineraries should include a little wine tasting, and we couldn’t wait to get started! Porto actually has a whole district called WOW (World of Wine), which occupies a complex of former port warehouses. It’s basically a complex of bars, restaurants, and museums, including a wine school where you can brush up on your knowledge of Portuguese vinho. Afternoon: River stroll + street performers + souvenir browsing Head back down towards the Douro and do a slow walk along the riverfront. This is prime people-watching territory: buskers, boat cruises, couples doing the “romantic photo” routine, and plenty of little souvenir stands. We picked up a couple of azulejo-style coffee cups here (zero regrets, and yes, we carried them like fragile babies for the rest of the trip). Snack stop: Pastries + Port If you’re hungry (or you just see it and get curious like we did), stop at Casa Portuguesa do Pastel de Bacalhau. We went in for the quirky decor and ended up staying longer because: there was a pianist playing live we got a fresh pastel de bacalhau (codfish cake) and honestly… port + salty snack is an elite combo There’s comfy seating upstairs, and it’s a great little reset before the evening. Evening: Sunset by the river If the weather behaves, aim for sunset around the river or back up near Jardim do Morro. Porto at golden hour is ridiculous (in the best way). For dinner, keep it easy: find a spot along the riverside for something unfussy and soak up the atmosphere. Day 1 is not the day to do a “serious meal” that requires spreadsheets and reservations — save that energy for Lisbon. Optional add-on (if you still have fuel in the tank): A short Douro Sunset River Cruise (especially nice if your legs are already protesting) Day 2: Porto (Historic Centre + viewpoints + dinner on the river) Day 2 of this road trip in Portugal is all about Porto’s historic centre — churches, azulejo tiles, viewpoints, and the kind of streets that make you stop every 30 seconds for photos. Morning: São Bento Station + Porto Cathedral Start at São Bento Train Station. Even if you don’t care about trains, the azulejo tile panels inside are one of Porto’s “yep, that’s why people come here” moments. From there, walk up to Porto Cathedral (Sé do Porto). It’s one of the city’s oldest landmarks, and the area around it has some great angles for photos over the rooftops and river. Practical tip: Porto is built on hills, and the old centre is full of uneven pavement. Wear shoes you can actually walk in — not your “cute but pointless” ones. Late morning: Livraria Lello + Igreja do Carmo For Potterheads, one of the highlights has to be the Livraria Lello, which is said to have inspired J. K. Rowling. Even if you’re not a fan of the books, it’s still worth pre-booking a ticket – it’s often cited as one of the most beautiful bookshops in the world! Afterwards, swing by Igreja do Carmo for more of Porto’s iconic tilework (your camera roll will basically become 90% azulejos at this point). Midday: Our favourite “real Porto” pocket (Largo da Pena Ventosa) One of our favourite places in Porto is the area around Largo da Pena Ventosa. It’s a super cute collection of narrow alleyways crisscrossed by drying laundry, giving it a traditional neighbourhood feel. Drop in on the small wine bar on the main square for a little glass of something and a snack. Afternoon: Palácio da Bolsa + Clérigos Tower Next, head to the Palácio da Bolsa (Stock Exchange Palace). It’s one of those places that surprises you — the interiors are seriously ornate, and the famous Arab Room is a standout. Then climb the 18th-century bell tower – Clérigos Church for one of the best viewpoints in Porto. Yes, it’s a workout, but the views are worth it. Optional (if you like evening culture): Clérigos often has evening performances inside the church — it’s a cool way to see the space in a different vibe than the daytime rush. Evening: Dinner on Cais da Ribeira (people-watching heaven) Finish the day with dinner along Cais da Ribeira, the riverside promenade. This area is touristy, yes — but it’s also genuinely fun at night. We ate at Ribeira 50. The food was solid, and the real reason to come is the location: perfect for sitting with a drink and watching the riverfront chaos unfold (street performers, passing boats, and that constant hum of Porto nightlife). If the weather turns moody (very Porto-like), don’t stress. We ended up sitting for ages with Portuguese wine, watching the rain and pretending it was all part of the plan. Day 3: Aveiro + Praia de Costa Nova Day 3 of your Portugal road trip (2-week route) is your first proper driving day: a quick stop in Aveiro, a coastal detour to Costa Nova, then onward to Nazaré. Morning: Drive Porto → Aveiro Set off from Porto and drive to Aveiro (just under an hour). It’s not a city you need to dedicate a whole day to, but it’s a perfect stop to stretch your legs and do something different before heading onwards. Parking (easy + central): The most convenient option we found was Parking Forum Aveiro — underground, paid, and right next to the historic centre. Park, forget the car exists for a few hours, and explore on foot. After you’ve ditched your wheels, stroll along the river, taking in the waterways and the unique local boats known as moliceiro. Traditionally, these long, narrow vessels with their brightly painted bows were used to harvest molico, a type of seaweed, but they’re now basically pleasure craft for tourists. ➡️⛵️If you want to do the canal tour, this is the moment — it’s an easy, low-effort activity after a drive. We booked ours in advance through Viator, selecting a 45-minute ride for €15 per person, which felt like decent value. Lunch: Urban Spot Cross the river via one of the many bridges and make your way up Aveiro’s main avenue, Doutor Lourenço Peixinho. We found a brunch place here called Urban Spot that does a fabulous stuffed croissant. Early afternoon: Wander the tiled streets Walk off your meal with a stroll down the city streets, which are paved with mosaic tiles. We kind of just let our feet go where they wanted, passing the stylish buildings of Praça do Doutor Joaquim de Melo Freitas and the Church of Aveiro’s Mercy. Afternoon: Drive to Praia da Costa Nova Before continuing to your next overnight stop, do the short detour to Praia da Costa Nova. Even if it’s not beach season, it’s still a classic trip moment: huge, wide beach, fresh sea air, and the famous striped colourful houses that look like someone designed them specifically for Instagram. There’s also a lighthouse here, and it’s an easy place to grab a few “Portugal coast” photos without committing to a full beach day. End of Day: Continue south to Nazaré After Costa Nova, hop back in the car and continue down to Nazaré for the night. Day 3 is deliberately light — you’re pacing the trip, not speed-running Portugal. Day 4: Nazaré + Óbidos (classic stops on a Portugal road trip) Day 4 is one of those “this is why we love a roadtripping Portugal: big Atlantic views in Nazaré, then a total vibe shift to medieval streets and city walls in Óbidos. It’s a great combo for a road trip in Portugal because neither place needs loads of time, but both feel super memorable. Morning: Nazaré big-wave viewpoint + beach walk Nazaré is famous for monster waves (especially in winter), and even if you’re not a surfer, it’s still seriously impressive to see the Atlantic doing its thing. Start at Farol de Nazaré (the lighthouse viewpoint). We went early and loved it — the views are dramatic, the air feels aggressively salty, and it’s a great “wake up, we’re on a road trip in Portugal!” moment. After the viewpoint, take a quick walk along Praia da Nazaré (the main beach). Even on a chill day, it’s a great place for photos and a coffee stop. Parking note: We found free parking near the lighthouse area, which made this stop ridiculously easy. Late morning: Drive Nazaré → Óbidos From Nazaré, it’s roughly 30 minutes to Óbidos. This is one of those drives where you barely settle in before you’re already pulling up again — perfect. Parking: Paid lot near the aqueduct (easy access) We parked in a paid lot near the aqueduct, a short walk to the old town entrance. It’s the simplest way to avoid stress, especially if you’re visiting mid-day when Óbidos gets busy. Midday: Porta da Vila + main street wander Enter through Porta da Vila, the tiled gate into the old town. It’s one of those places that instantly makes you want to slow down. When we arrived, a musician was playing, and the acoustics under the arch were weirdly good — like a mini concert for random passers-by. From there, stroll along Rua Direita, the main pedestrian street lined with small shops, cafés, and plenty of places selling ginja (sour cherry liqueur). It’s touristy, yes, but it’s also genuinely fun. Afternoon: Walk the city walls + Castelo de Óbidos Óbidos’ medieval city walls are one of the best parts — and they’re free to access. The views over the rooftops and countryside are fantastic. Important: there are sections with no guardrails, so watch your step and don’t try to do it while juggling a drink, a camera, and questionable shoes (we’ve learned the hard way in other places). Overlooking the town is Castelo de Óbidos, a proper storybook castle that’s now a hotel. Even if you’re not staying, it’s worth seeing from the outside while you’re wandering around — it gives the whole place that “medieval fairytale” feel. Late afternoon/evening: Head toCascais After exploring Óbidos, we continued our road trip to Cascais for the night. It’s an easy drive, and staying here makes the next two days (Cascais + Sintra) much less rushed. Plus, it’s genuinely nice to arrive somewhere coastal again after a couple of inland-ish stops. Day 5: Cascais & Cape Roca Day 5 of this Portugal road trip itinerary (2 weeks) is pure coastal therapy: pretty streets, sea views, and a quick hop out to Cabo da Roca — the westernmost point of mainland Europe. Staying overnight in Cascais is also a sneaky-smart move for a road trip in Portugal, because it sets you up perfectly for Sintra tomorrow without a long commute. Morning: Explore Cascais (old town + waterfront) Start with a slow wander through Cascais Old Town. It’s compact, walkable, and full of those “accidentally cute” corners — tiled façades, little cafés, and boutique shops you swear you’ll “just pop into for two minutes”. Walk down towards the waterfront and Praia da Ribeira de Cascais (the main beach). Even if you don’t swim, it’s a great place to sit for a bit and watch the world go by. Late morning: Museum Quarter + palace-museum One of the nicest pockets in Cascais is the area around the Citadel of Cascais (a fortress-turned-palace-turned cultural space). We found parking nearby, then explored on foot. If you like old houses with character (and slightly chaotic collections), don’t miss the Museu Condes de Castro Guimarães. It’s part mini-palace, part treasure chest — and it’s one of the most interesting indoor stops in Cascais. Just across the way, stop at the Miradouro Casa de Santa Maria for the classic view over the lighthouse and the water. Quick, easy, and very photogenic. Afternoon: Cabo da Roca (windy, dramatic, worth it) Next, drive out to Cabo da Roca. The coastline here feels wild compared to the polished Riviera vibe of Cascais — rugged cliffs, big Atlantic wind, and the kind of views that make you go quiet for a minute. It’s not a long stop (unless you’re the type who likes staring into the distance, having a “main character moment”), but it’s a great one to tick off on this route because it’s genuinely unique. Tip: bring a layer. Even if it’s warm in town, Cabo da Roca can be weirdly cold and windy. Evening: Sunset + overnight in Cascais Wrap the day back in Cascais with a sunset stroll on the promenade, then dinner somewhere in town. The big win: sleep in Cascais tonight. It makes tomorrow’s Sintra day so much easier — you can go early, time it around the weather, and you’re not commuting from Lisbon with the rest of humanity. Day 6: Sintra Day Trip (from Cascais) Day 6 is one of the biggest highlights of this Portugal itinerary (2 weeks): Sintra. It’s a fairytale hill town packed with palaces, forests, and views — and it’s also the day when planning actually matters. Doing Sintra as a day trip from Cascais is ideal, because you’re close enough to arrive early and beat some crowds. Morning: Arrive early + get up to Pena Palace Start early and head straight to Pena Palace (National Palace of Pena). It’s the most famous sight in Sintra for a reason — colourful, dramatic, and sitting up on the hill like it’s showing off. Our honest take: the outside is the wow-factor. The inside is fine, but it’s not the main event. Crowd tip: if you’re choosing a timed entry, the earliest or latest slots can be great for photos because people start thinning out. We booked late once and got surprisingly calm courtyard shots. Late morning: Moorish Castle (our favourite part) Next, head to the Moorish Castle (Castelo dos Mouros). If you like views and a bit of adventure, this is the one not to skip. Walking along the walls and towers was genuinely one of our favourite things we did in Sintra — it feels ancient, windy, and epic in the best way. Wear proper shoes here. The paths and steps aren’t “cute sandal” terrain. Lunch: A low-key local spot Between palaces, stop for lunch in town. We ate at Cajo (a cosy neighbourhood restaurant), and it was exactly what we needed: relaxed, tasty, and not a tourist-trap circus. Sintra can feel like constant uphill walking + timed tickets, so a calm lunch break makes a huge difference. Afternoon: Pick one more sight (don’t try to do them all) Sintra is where people get over-ambitious and then end the day slightly dead inside. Realistically, after Pena + the Moorish Castle, pick one extra place depending on your energy: National Palace of Sintra (the one with the iconic twin chimneys), if you want something central and easy Or a quieter palace/estate if you’re feeling “more gardens, less crowds” Quick note: you can’t just drive between the main sights easily. The area is busy, roads are tight, and parking is limited — which is why we recommend doing what we did: park in town and use local transport. Late afternoon: Head back to Cascais (easy win) After a full day of hills, viewpoints, and palace steps, we went back to Cascais for the night. Day 7: Lisbon (Baixa, Alfama + the “must see in Lisbon” classics) Day 7 is when this Portugal itinerary shifts into city mode. Did you know that Lisbon is the second-oldest capital in Europe, older even than Rome? No, neither did we before our visit! Morning Drive: Cascais → Lisbon + park the car From Cascais, it’s an easy hop into Lisbon. Our biggest tip: don’t drive around central Lisbon unless you enjoy steep streets and confusing one-ways. If your hotel has parking, use it. If not, use a paid underground car park near where you’re staying and leave the car there until you’re ready to head to Évora. Late morning: Rossio + Santa Justa Lift (go early) Start around Rossio Square, which is a great “base point” for your first day in Lisbon. Next: Santa Justa Lift. The town authorities even built an elevator in 1902 to make it easier for citizens to travel between upper and lower Lisbon. It’s one of those attractions that’s both useful and a bit of a novelty. It can get painfully busy, so try to go earlier in the day if you want to avoid a long queue. We’ll be honest: we loved it… But we loved it more when we weren’t standing in line behind 200 people who all had the same idea. 😅 Midday: Rua Augusta → Arco da Rua Augusta → Praça do Comércio Walk down Rua Augusta, the big pedestrian street lined with shops and restaurants. It’s not a “destination” in itself, but it’s a great way to absorb the vibe of central Lisbon. At the end, you’ll hit: Arco da Rua Augusta (a dramatic arch you can’t miss, it commemorates the reconstruction of Lisbon after a lot of it was levelled by an earthquake in 1755.) Praça do Comércio (the big waterfront square that feels like Lisbon’s front porch) This is a good point to grab a coffee, sit for a bit, and do some people-watching. Afternoon: Tram 28 + Alfama + our favourite viewpoint Lisbon’s hills are no joke, so this is where we shamelessly use the city’s most iconic transport: Tram 28. Yes, it’s touristy. Yes, it’s still fun. Get off for Alfama, Lisbon’s oldest-feeling neighbourhood — narrow lanes, little staircases, and viewpoints that make you stop mid-sentence. If you only do one viewpoint today, make it Miradouro de Santa Luzia. We loved it: beautiful azulejos, a balcony vibe, and a classic view over the rooftops towards the river. If you’ve still got energy, head up to Castelo de São Jorge for more views (and more steps… always more steps). Tip: Lisbon will trick you. Everything looks close on the map, but the hills turn a “15-minute walk” into a mini workout. Evening: Time Out Market + grilled squid + Pink Street End the day somewhere easy and lively: Time Out Market is perfect for that. Lots of food options under one roof, minimal decision fatigue, and it’s great when you’re hungry but can’t agree on what you want. While you’re there (or anywhere around the waterfront), try grilled squid. We ordered it on a whim, and it was super tasty — smoky, salty, and surprisingly tender when it’s done right. It’s exactly the kind of simple seafood dish that just tastes better in Portugal. After dinner, swing by Pink Street nearby — it’s a quick, fun look at Lisbon nightlife without committing to a full night out. Day 8: Lisbon & Belém (Monastery, Tower + the best pastel de nata) Today is all about Belém, Lisbon’s grand waterfront district, plus one of the most iconic food stops in the country. Morning: Jerónimos Monastery (go early) Start at Jerónimos Monastery. It’s genuinely one of the most impressive buildings we visited on our whole Portugal road trip — the stonework is insanely detailed. Queue tip: go early (or later in the day). We arrived in the morning and waited for around half an hour, but the lines can get much worse. If you’re visiting in peak season, booking ahead can save your sanity. Late morning: Belém Tower (outside = must, inside = optional) Next, walk over to Belém Tower. The outside is absolutely worth it — classic Lisbon postcard material. Our honest take: we didn’t find the inside nearly as interesting as the exterior. If the queue looks brutal, you can skip going in and still feel like you’ve “done” Belém. Midday: Pastéis de Belém (yes it’s busy, yes do it anyway) Now for the important cultural activity: Pastéis de Belém. It’s crowded. It’s chaotic. It’s also one of the most iconic food stops in Portugal, so just embrace it and get your custard tart (or three). The staff are used to the volume, and it moves faster than it looks from the outside. Pro tip: Grab a table inside if you can. It’s a nice little break after walking around Belém, and the fresh ones hit differently when you’re sitting down with a coffee. Afternoon: Tram to LX Factory (Lisbon’s cool “industrial-hipster” stop) After Belém, hop on a tram/taxi and head to LX Factory. It’s a former industrial complex turned into a trendy zone of cafés, restaurants, shops, and street art — the vibe is on point, especially if you want a break from churches and monuments. It’s great for: browsing little boutiques grabbing a drink casual snacks and generally wandering around saying “we should totally live here” (we say that in every city, to be fair 😅) Evening: Back into central Lisbon Head back into central Lisbon for dinner. If you’re feeling tired (likely), do something simple near your hotel — tomorrow is a driving day towards Évora, so you’ll thank yourself for not going too hard tonight Day 9: Évora (Best Inland Stop on a 2-Week Portugal Road Trip) Day 9 is where your Portugal road trip itinerary takes a little detour inland — and it’s so worth it. After a few days of Lisbon, Évora feels like stepping into a postcard: medieval lanes, ancient ruins, tiled churches, and one of the creepiest (but most memorable) sights.. Morning: Drive Lisbon → Évora + park The drive from Lisbon to Évora is easy and makes for a nice change after city walking. Parking tip: aim for a paid lot just outside the historic centre (easy in/out), then walk in. It keeps your stress levels low and your day enjoyable. Late morning: Aqueduct + Rua do Cano (the iconic “walk under it” street) Start at the 16th-century Aqueduct of Évora and follow Rua do Cano into town — this is one of those “wow, the aqueduct is literally built into the street” moments that make you stop mid-walk for photos. Midday: Roman Temple + slow wander through the historic centre Right in the centre of things is one of the city’s oldest landmarks, the Roman Temple of Evora. Although there’s not much to the ruin these days, it’s a very dramatic building to have in the middle of a square. On your way to the next stop, pass through Giraldo Square — it’s Évora’s main plaza and a good spot for a coffee break and people watching. afternoon: the Chapel of Bones + University of Évora + Royal Palace gardens Évora has some gorgeous religious buildings, but the standout “did we really just see that?” stop is the Chapel of Bones. It’s lined with real human skeletons — equal parts fascinating and grim. It’s not a long visit, but it’s definitely memorable. Just a short walk from the Chapel of Bones is Portugal’s second-oldest university. Established in 1559, the University of Evora is open to the public, which means you can poke your nose into tile-decorated classrooms – when there aren’t classes, of course. A street or two over, you can also see what remains of the Royal Palace of Evora. The building itself isn’t overly impressive, but the surrounding gardens are a nice place to go for a time out. Late afternoon (best timing): Évora Cathedral rooftop (our favourite) Save Évora Cathedral for later in the day if you can. We went up in the late afternoon, close to closing time, and it felt noticeably quieter than earlier. The rooftop views are the real reason to go — we spent ages up there taking photos and enjoying the stunning architecture. This was hands down our favourite part of Évora. Evening: Dinner at O Templo For dinner, we ate at O Templo, and it ended up being one of the best meals of our whole trip. We didn’t have a reservation (bold move), so we showed up right at opening and managed to snag the last free table, sharing the moment with another couple who’d had the same idea. The rest of the restaurant was already pre-booked, so if you’re visiting in high season, either reserve ahead or copy our strategy and arrive early. Order the pork cheeks stewed in red wine if they’re available — genuinely outstanding. Day 10: Costa Vicentina Road (Estrada da Praia) + Sagres Day 10 is one of the most “this is why we rented a car” days on this Portugal itinerary. You’re heading into the wilder coastline of the Costa Vicentina, driving the scenic Estrada da Praia route, then finishing in Sagres for cliffs, sea air, and sunset energy. If you’re doing a road trip in Portugal, this is the day that makes the whole thing feel like a proper adventure. Morning: Drive Évora → Costa Vicentina (longest drive of the trip) This is your longest drive day — just over 3 hours — so start reasonably early. Bordeira Beach. Late morning: Start the Estrada da Praia loop (viewpoints + beaches) The Estrada da Praia is essentially a coastal dirt track that runs along a seriously beautiful stretch of coastline. There are multiple signed stopping points (marked with letters), each with free parking and quick viewpoints. Even though it’s a dirt road, we found it well-maintained and did it comfortably in a small car (we were in a VW Polo). Just take it slow and don’t treat it like a rally stage. Along the loop, stop at beaches like: Bordeira Beach (huge, windy, dramatic) Praia do Amado (classic surf beach vibe) This part of the trip is very much: pull over → stare at the ocean → take photos → repeat. Afternoon: Drive to Sagres (small town, big coastline) After the coastal loop, drive about 30 minutes south to Sagres. The town itself is small, but it’s a great base for exploring the cliffs and headlands around the southwestern tip of Portugal. If you’re into history, you can also check out the 15th-century fortress associated with Henry the Navigator — it’s a quick, atmospheric stop, and the location is the main event. Late afternoon/sunset: Cabo de São Vicente (go before peak sunset chaos) Head out to Cabo de São Vicente, the southwesternmost point of mainland Europe. It’s stunning — but it’s also popular at sunset, so we recommend going a bit earlier if you want the views without full-on crowds. Parking tip: Parking can be a struggle at the cape, so if you have the time and the energy, do what we did and hike the 7.4km (4.6 miles) trail from Sagres. It takes about two hours, but it’s a nice walk. Plus, you can catch the bus back to save you from making the return journey on foot! Evening: Sleep in Lagos (better Algarve base) Rather than staying in Sagres, we drove about 30 minutes along the coast to Lagos, which is a more practical base for the Algarve portion of this 2 weeks in Portugal itinerary. You’ll be glad you did — Lagos makes the next few days much easier. Day 11: Lagos, Ponta de Piedade hike & Dona Ana Beach Day 11 is peak Algarve: Lagos old town, the Ponta da Piedade coastal walk, and proper beach time — basically the ideal Algarve itinerary. For a shorter south-only route, see our Algarve road trip itinerary, plus our guide to renting a car in the Algarve for practical driving and parking tips. Morning: Lagos Old Town (easy stroll + a little culture) Start your day in the Old Town of Lagos, a cobblestoned area that is partially circumscribed by medieval walls. Make sure to check out the Church of Saint Anthony, a simple but attractive building that conceals some super-bling wood carvings. Next, head to Porta de São Gonçalo, which you can pass through to get to the well-preserved Forte da Ponta da Bandeira and a sandy beach broken up by rock formations. Afternoon: Ponta da Piedade hike We were still craving more nature, so we walked a short way out of town (about 15-20 minutes) to the starting point of the Ponda da Piedade hike. This boardwalk trail curves around the coast outside of Lagos, passing hidden beaches like Praia do Camilo and viewpoints like the Miradouro do Abismo. Grab a freshly squeezed OJ at O Camilo en route – it was delicious and a great pick-me-up. Mid/late afternoon: Praia Dona Ana (swim + late lunch) After the hike, head down to Praia Dona Ana, one of the prettiest beaches around Lagos. It’s a classic Algarve scene — golden sand, cliffs, and bright water when the sun’s out. For a casual meal, we ate at Marisol, a beachfront spot that was decently priced and perfect for a post-walk refuel. Evening: Sunset + dinner in Lagos Finish the day back in Lagos with an easy dinner in town. You’ll find loads of options around the centre. Day 12: Benagil Cave & Carvoeiro Day 12 is a classic Algarve combo: a morning on the water at Benagil Cave, then a slower afternoon in Carvoeiro with cliffs, boardwalk views, and that relaxed beach-town feel. Morning: Drive Lagos → Benagil + take a tour (don’t swim) Start early and drive from Lagos to Benagil (about 45 minutes). The Benagil Cave is one of the Algarve’s most famous natural sights — a huge sea cave with a sandy “hidden beach” inside and a circular opening in the roof that lets the light pour in. To get there, you need to go by sea. The most common options are: Kayak tour (what we did — fun and active) Paddleboard tour (more balance required… good luck 😅) Boat tour (best if you want something easy and dry) Important: Don’t try to swim to the cave. The currents here can be dangerous and people drown every year. After your tour, take a breather nearby — even a short walk by the beach feels great after paddling. Afternoon: Carvoeiro (easy stroll + cliff views) Benagil Cave is just outside the resort town of Carvoeiro, a lovely little place with a sandy beach, orange cliffs, and white-washed houses. There are a few shops to browse in town, but the main point of coming here is to chill by the sea. If it’s too brisk to swim, there’s a great boardwalk that goes past a series of caves and rock formations. Evening: Sunset in Carvoeiro or back in Lagos Depending on your energy, you can: stay for sunset in Carvoeiro, then drive back to Lagos, or head back earlier and have a chill dinner in Lagos Either way, keep it light — tomorrow has another couple of beautiful Algarve towns and it’s easy to over-pack these days if you’re not careful. Day 13: Ferragudo & Portimao Day 13 is a great Portugal road trip day because you get two totally different vibes close together: Ferragudo (small, charming, photogenic and our fav!) and Portimão (bigger, busier, more “holiday town”). Morning: Ferragudo (cobbled streets + viewpoint wander) Start in Ferragudo, a small village with cobblestone streets, colourful houses, and flowers spilling over balconies like it’s trying to win an award for “cutest place in the Algarve”. This is a wander-and-snack kind of stop: stroll the lanes slowly (Ferragudo is tiny, in a good way) stop when you see a cute terrace take a million photos without even trying Late morning: Benjamim Bistro (desserts happen) We stopped at Benjamim Bistro and fully leaned into dessert mode. The cake counter is dangerously convincing, and sitting outside with coffee and something sweet was peak holiday energy. If you’re doing this day with a car, Ferragudo is also the kind of place where you can park, walk around for a couple of hours, and not feel rushed. Ferragudo seaside. Afternoon: Portimão (marina + beaches) Next, head across to Portimão. It’s larger and more built-up, and we didn’t find the historic centre particularly special — if you’re short on time, don’t stress about lingering there. The better parts of Portimão are: the marina area (livelier, nicer for a stroll) the beach zone (more of a “proper resort” vibe) Evening: Back to Lagos Head back to Lagos for dinner — it’s easy and you’ll already know your favourite streets by now. Day 14: Albufeira Old Town & Dos Pescadores Beach (Final Algarve Day) Day 14 is the last day of your 2 weeks in Portugal, and yes — Albufeira has a party reputation (especially with Brits), but the Old Town is actually pretty charming when you focus on the right spots. Miradouro do Pau da Bandeira. Morning: Albufeira Old Town wander (keep it simple) Start in Albufeira Old Town, where the streets are pedestrian-friendly and lined with cafés and shops. It’s a good place for a slow morning stroll and a coffee without committing to a full “tourist checklist” day. Late morning: Miradouro do Pau da Bandeira (best easy viewpoint) Head to Miradouro do Pau da Bandeira for one of the best views over Albufeira’s whitewashed houses and the beach. One of the underrated perks here: you can get up to the viewpoint using an escalator from the Old Town. No sweaty hill climb required. We love a scenic view that doesn’t demand cardio. Midday: Photos + lunch in the Old Town Spend a bit of time around Largo Engenheiro Duarte Pacheco, the main square — it’s a nice spot for photos and has plenty of outdoor seating nearby. For lunch, pick an outdoor terrace and keep it relaxed. If you want a specific option, we ate at Alfredo and had a really solid seafood pasta, with a great “watch the world go by” setup. Afternoon: Praia dos Pescadores (beach time + final drink) End your trip properly at Praia dos Pescadores, the big beach right below the Old Town. It’s easy, lively, and lined with beach bars where you can grab a beer or cocktail as your unofficial road trip closing ceremony. Optional: Sunset finish If you can time it, stay until sunset. Albufeira gets busy, but the golden light over the coastline is a strong final memory to take home. Do I need a car to visit Portugal?A car isn’t essential if you’re only doing the big cities, but it’s a game-changer for a road trip in Portugal (especially the Algarve beaches, viewpoints, and smaller towns). For city logistics and pick-up tips, we also cover this in our renting a car in Lisbon guide. Is Portugal good for a road trip?Yes — it’s one of the easiest “first-timer” road trips in Europe: decent roads, straightforward navigation, and loads of variety in a small-ish country. If you end up loving the driving side of it, Madeira is another favourite of ours — see our Madeira road trip itinerary and renting a car in Madeira guide for an island-style version. Where should I start a 2 week Portugal road trip: Porto, Lisbon, or Faro?All work. For this 2 week itinerary, starting in Porto and finishing in the Algarve makes the route feel nicely “north to south”. But starting in Lisbon (or Faro) is totally fine too — just flip the order based on flights and car prices. Can I do this itinerary without a car?Partially. You can do Porto and Lisbon easily without a car, and you can reach some towns by train/bus — but the more scenic bits (Costa Vicentina viewpoints, beach-hopping, quick detours) are where a car saves time and hassle. How do tolls work on a road trip in Portugal?Portugal has toll roads, and some are electronic. With a rental car, the easiest setup is usually a toll device/system (often Via Verde-style) so charges are recorded automatically and billed later. Ask at pick-up how it works for your specific rental so you don’t accidentally collect toll drama. Is parking difficult in Porto and Lisbon?In the historic centres, yes — it can be tight, steep, and not worth the effort. Our approach: park at the hotel (or a paid garage) and explore on foot/metro/Uber. Then use the car for the “road trip” days, not the city days. How long would it take to drive around Portugal?We took it slow, but if you drove straight from north to south on highways, it’s roughly a half-day drive. If you avoid toll roads and take coastal routes, add extra time — and honestly, the slower route is usually the prettier one. Can I do this Portugal road trip in 10 days instead of 2 weeks?Yes — but you’ll need to cut at least one base. The easiest trims are: fewer Lisbon days, skip Évora, or simplify the Algarve stops. Another good option is doing a focused Algarve itinerary only. Can I combine Spain and Portugal in 2 weeks?You can, but it gets rushed fast unless you keep Spain to one region (like Andalusia) and streamline Portugal. If you want a calmer trip with less packing and more enjoying, two weeks is honestly perfect for Portugal alone. Final Word Two weeks is the sweet spot for a Portugal road trip: long enough to cover the big hitters (Porto, Lisbon, the Algarve) without turning every day into a race. If you follow this route, you’ll get a proper mix of cities, coastal scenery, and a few slower, “we didn’t plan this, but it was amazing” moments — which is exactly how Portugal shines.
